description: Wrists that hurt in push-ups and planks are usually undertrained for load, not fragile. Take the tabletop weight-bearing test, learn how wrist tendons heal through graded loading, and get the plan that earns your wrists their strength back without a single stretch forced through pain.

scenes.narration: Get on all fours on something soft, palms flat under your shoulders, fingers pointing forward, and slowly lean your weight into your hands until your wrists are carrying as much as they honestly accept. Start the clock. Hold that honest load, breathing normally, no shaking it out, until the ache reaches a four out of ten or your form folds. That is your number: the seconds your wrists can bear real weight. If you had to come off in under ten seconds, do not be annoyed, be informed: push-ups, planks, and handstands have been asking your wrists for a load they have never been trained to hold. Keep your seconds safe. At the end of this video, I will tell you what they mean.

scenes.label: SECONDS OF HONEST WEIGHT-BEARING
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Forty five seconds of honest tabletop weight-bearing is where a wrist stops being the reason you avoid the floor and starts being a platform you can build on. Under twenty, the tendons and small structures of the wrist are simply unpracticed at load, whatever their flexibility looks like in a stretch. Between twenty and forty five, capacity is real but thin, and one ambitious workout can spend it all. Over ninety, your wrists hold what calisthenics actually asks: full push-up sets, long planks, and the first honest handstand work. Notice that this number is not about how far the wrist bends. It is about how much the bent wrist can carry. That difference runs this whole video.
scenes.sub: under 20: unpracticed at load - over 90: push-up proof

scenes.narration: Look at the engineering you are standing on. The wrist is a bridge of eight small bones in two rows, crossed on both sides by tendon cables running from your forearm muscles out to your fingers. There is almost no muscle inside the wrist itself. The strength of the whole structure is its suspension: tendons above and below, tensioning the bridge from both directions every time you load it. When those tendons are untrained, the bridge takes load passively, bone on bone and ligament on ligament, and the ache you feel is the structure complaining about working without its suspension crew. Healing wrist tendons is not about oiling the bridge. It is about hiring the crew: graded pressing loads that teach the forearm tendons to tension the wrist from both sides, a little more each week, until the bridge carries weight the way it was designed to.

lines: legal ways to shrink the dose.
beats.title: DOSE KNOBS

scenes.narration: Now the principle that makes wrist healing work where stretching fails. A sore wrist has two separate problems people constantly confuse: it may lack angle, the last degrees of bend, and it may lack load capacity at whatever angle it has. Training them in the wrong order is the classic mistake. Full angle on day one, palms flat in a hard plank, is the maximum dose delivered to the least prepared tissue. The order that heals is the reverse: load first, at partial angles the wrist accepts, using fists, fingertips, or an incline to shrink the dose. Capacity grows there for a few weeks. Then the last degrees of angle get earned by a structure that is finally strong enough to own them. Angle follows strength. Every wrist that ever healed for real followed that order, whether its owner knew it or not.

One more mechanism, and it is free. Squeeze something hard and feel your whole forearm light up, front and back at once. That is co-contraction: the tendons on both sides of the wrist firing together, and it is the exact pattern that stabilizes the bridge under load. This is why grip work secretly heals wrists. Every strong squeeze rehearses the suspension crew in its working formation, at loads the wrist can choose for itself. It is also why your wrists feel worse in the exercises where your fingers are spread and passive, like a lazy plank, than in the ones where your hands are active. An active hand is a stabilized wrist. A passive hand is a bridge with the crew on break. From today, every grip you train is also wrist rehab, and every plank you do with fingers clawing the floor is a different, kinder exercise for the same joints.

Here is the skinny advantage at the wrist. Weight-bearing dose is your bodyweight, and yours is the smaller prescription. A heavy guy leaning into a tabletop loads his wrists with a sledgehammer; you load yours with a tool you can adjust by leaning an inch forward or back. That fine knob is everything in graded loading, because healing lives in the narrow band between too little and too much, and you can park inside that band precisely, every day, on any floor. No dumbbells, no machines, no wrist gadgets. Just lean, hold, breathe, and let the suspension crew clock in. Your wrists will never be the strongest part of a heavy lifter's highlight reel. They can absolutely become the most reliable part of yours.

Train with me. All fours, palms flat, lean in until the wrists work honestly but stay under a three out of ten. Thirty seconds on, twenty off, three rounds. Fists instead of palms is a legal easier version today.

Here is your week. Tabletop bearing practice every day, short holds at an honest load, leaning a little further only when the current lean feels boring. Grip work three days a week, squeezes and hangs, knowing it is secretly wrist day too. Push-ups move to an incline or to fists until the flat-palm version is earned. The ladder is fingertips, then palms at an incline, then palms on the floor, one rung a week at most. The mistakes to retire: forcing full palm planks because the program says so, retired. Stretching the wrist hard into end range before it can bear weight, retired. Wearing a brace all day and calling it healing, retired; a brace is a rest, not a repair. And the rule: if one specific spot stays tender, if there is clicking with pain, numbness in the fingers, or a wrist that swells, see a professional if it persists. Those details change the diagnosis, and diagnosis changes everything.

So, your seconds. Under twenty: your wrists are unpracticed at load, not fragile, and the daily bearing work was built for exactly this start. Twenty to forty five: the suspension crew is clocking in, keep the lean creeping forward and let grip days do their double duty. Over forty five: your wrists are load-ready, and the floor is yours again, push-ups first, handstand dreams after. Comment your seconds, just the number. In thirty days we lean in again and see how long the bridge holds. Wrists do not heal by being avoided. They heal by being loaded like they matter, because they do.

Your wrists carry your whole training life. They just needed to be trained like it. Lean in a little every day, and in thirty days we hold the bridge together again. Subscribe so the retest finds you. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Stop Doing wrist pain Wrong: Train Your wrist tendon healing Instead
